title: Jubilees
subtitle: Genesis and Exodus retold from the heavenly tablets, dated in jubilees
lead: Jubilees retells Genesis 1 to Exodus 24, from the six days of creation to the giving of the law on Mount Sinai. It presents itself as what the angel of the presence dictated to Moses during his forty days on the mountain, copied from the heavenly tablets (1:27; 2:1). Every event is dated in jubilees of 49 years and in weeks of years, and the patriarchs are shown already keeping laws that Moses would later receive: the Sabbath, the Feast of Weeks, circumcision on the eighth day, tithes and purity. It has 50 chapters, 1,307 verses and a short prologue.

It is not in most Bibles. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts it as Scripture, under the name Kufale ("Division"), and the whole book survives only in Ge'ez, that church's ancient language. Jews, Catholics, the Eastern Orthodox and Protestants do not count it as Scripture. Yet it matters to all of them. It was written in Hebrew in the 100s BC, copies were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Damascus Document names it, and it shows how one priestly circle read Genesis and Exodus a century or two before Jesus: R. H. Charles called it "the oldest commentary in the world on Genesis."
facts: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose list of 81 books names it among the 46 of the Old Testament ("Jublee"). It shaped the calendar and practice of the Beta Israel, Ethiopia's Jews (Encyclopaedia Judaica). Not Scripture for Jews, Catholics, Eastern Orthodox or Protestants.
The book says the angel of the presence dictated it and Moses wrote it on Mount Sinai (1:5; 1:27; 2:1). Most scholars: an unknown Jewish writer, very likely a priest, of the 100s BC.

Most scholars now: about 170–140 BC (VanderKam). R. H. Charles: 135 to about 105 BC, under John Hyrcanus. G. W. E. Nickelsburg and J. Goldstein: before 167 BC (as VanderKam reports them). Before the Dead Sea Scrolls, many dated it to the first century AD.
Mount Sinai in the first year after the Exodus; the story it tells runs from creation to Sinai.
Hebrew. Fragments of Hebrew copies were found in the Qumran caves.

Ge'ez (complete; the four manuscripts Charles used included two of the 1400s and 1500s; 27 copies were known by 1992); Latin (about a quarter of the book, in one palimpsest); Greek (lost, known from quotations in church writers and Byzantine chroniclers); Hebrew fragments from the Dead Sea Scrolls; a Syriac list of the patriarchs' wives.
Rewritten Bible: a retelling of Genesis and Exodus with added laws, dates, speeches, testaments and a vision of the last days (23:8–32)
50 chapters, 1,307 verses, plus a prologue (printed here as verse 1:0)
authorship: The book's own claim and the Ethiopian Orthodox reading

Jubilees says God told Moses to write in a book what he heard on the mountain (1:5), then told the angel of the presence to write for Moses from the beginning of creation (1:27), and the angel speaks as "we," one of the angels who saw it all. So the words come from heaven, through an angel, to Moses. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church keeps the book in its Old Testament, next to Enoch, after the Chronicles, and calls it the book of "Division" or the "Little Genesis." Read this way, Jubilees is the fuller account of what Moses learned on Sinai, and Genesis and Exodus are the shorter.

Almost all scholars see an unknown Jewish author writing in Hebrew in the 100s BC, who put his teaching in the mouth of Moses and an angel. R. H. Charles (1902) argued he was a Pharisee who supported the Maccabean high priests and was probably a priest himself, writing between 135 BC (when John Hyrcanus became high priest) and Hyrcanus's break with the Pharisees, before 105 BC. Once Qumran copies were dated by their handwriting to about 100 BC, that date became too late. James VanderKam (1992) puts the book between about 170 and 140 BC, by a priest whose laws are closer to what is known of the Essenes than to the Pharisees or Sadducees. Yehoshua Grintz (Encyclopaedia Judaica) places the author at the end of Hyrcanus's reign.

Before the Dead Sea Scrolls, opinion ranged widely, as Charles lists it: Dillmann dated it to the first century AD before the fall of Jerusalem; Rönsch to AD 50–60, as a Jewish work against the rising church; Singer to about AD 58–60, as a Jewish Christian work against Paul; Beer thought a Samaritan wrote it; Frankel tied it to the Jewish temple at Leontopolis in Egypt; Jellinek thought it Essene; and Krüger dated it to 320 BC. The Qumran copies ruled out the first-century dates.

audience.to: Jews in the land of Israel in the 100s BC, in the years after the Greek ways that the high priest Jason and King Antiochus IV had pushed on Judea (1 Maccabees 1; 2 Maccabees 4), and very likely a priestly circle. Inside the story, the hearer is Moses on Mount Sinai, and through him all Israel, who are told what their fathers did and what they themselves will do. The first real readers we can name are the people who kept the book at Qumran: Hebrew fragments of it were found in at least five caves there, Caves 1, 2, 3, 4 and 11 (Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library), and the Damascus Document, a rule book of the same movement, sends its readers to "the Book of Time Divisions by Jubilees and Weeks" for the exact times of Israel's blindness (CD 16:2–4, Cook's translation).
audience.why: R. H. Charles read the book as an answer to Jews drawn to Greek ways, for whom the law of Moses was a late and passing thing; that is a reading of the evidence, since the date and the first readers are debated (see below). On that reading, its answer is that the law is older than Moses: it was written on the heavenly tablets before the world, kept by the angels in heaven, and kept by the patriarchs on earth. Enoch kept the calendar, Noah kept the Feast of Weeks, Abraham kept the Feast of Booths and circumcised on the eighth day, Levi was made a priest and took tithes. So the law cannot be set aside as Israel's young custom, and those who drop circumcision, the Sabbath or the true calendar, or who marry outside Israel, are not modern but lost. Charles put it as a defense of Judaism against the Greek spirit and a proof that the law was "of everlasting validity." Knowing the readers changes the reading. The many dates and laws are not dry detail: they are the writer's way of saying that Israel's way of life is built into creation itself.
views: Jews loyal to the law after the Maccabean revolt

Charles read the book as written in the strong days of the Maccabean rulers, for Jews who had seen the persecution of Antiochus IV and still faced the pull of Greek culture. He saw the period in the laws against nakedness (3:31, aimed at the Greek games), on circumcision (15:33–34), on the Sabbath (50:12, no war), and against intermarriage (30:7–17), and in the wars against Edom and the Amorites (34; 37–38).
Jews before or during the revolt

Nickelsburg and Goldstein argue that the book was written before 167 BC, before the worst of the persecution (as VanderKam reports them); VanderKam places it between about 170 and 140 BC, and notes that the Maccabean allusions others see (for example in 23:20) can be read other ways.
A priestly group close to the Essenes and Qumran

VanderKam thinks a priest wrote it, since the book exalts Levi and traces priestly law through a line of righteous men, and that the author probably belonged to the movement later called the Essenes. The Qumran copies, the shared 364-day calendar, and the Damascus Document's reference fit this. VanderKam (1992) counted fragments of twelve manuscripts; Matthew Monger (2014), studying the copy 4Q216, argues that "there were likely not 14 complete manuscripts of Jubilees at Qumran," and Devorah Dimant has questioned whether the Damascus Document's words are really a quotation of Jubilees, so how central the book was there is debated.

lenses.name: Ethiopian Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church reads Kufale as Scripture in its Old Testament: the account of what was revealed to Moses on Sinai, read with the Orit (the books of Moses) and handed down in Ge'ez.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read it as a Jewish rewriting of Genesis and Exodus made in Hebrew in the 100s BC, and ask what it argued, against whom: the calendar, circumcision, the Sabbath, marriage to outsiders, and the place of the priests.

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: Readers who use it to understand the world of the New Testament: the law given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2), Sabbath and calendar debates, Abraham's faith and testing, demons and their prince, and the Watchers as Jude and 2 Peter knew them.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: How Jews used it: copied at Qumran and named in the Damascus Document; set aside by the rabbis, whose calendar and laws differ; echoed in later midrash such as Midrash Tadshe and the medieval Book of Jashar; and kept by the Beta Israel of Ethiopia.

lenses.name: Most churches: useful, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Protestant readers: an early Jewish witness to how Genesis and Exodus were read before Christ, to be tested against the Bible rather than read as the Bible.

sections.b:
Read it with Genesis and Exodus open. Jubilees follows them closely, often word for word, and the interest is in what it adds, cuts and changes. The notes mark each retold verse and say plainly where Jubilees matches the Bible, goes beyond it, or conflicts with it.

Watch for three things that run through the whole book. Time: every event has a date in jubilees and weeks of years, and the year has 364 days (6:32), so that the feasts always fall on the same day of the week. Law before Sinai: again and again the angel says a law is "written on the heavenly tablets," and the patriarchs keep it long before Moses. Israel set apart: the Sabbath, circumcision and marriage inside the family of Jacob mark Israel off from the nations, which God has placed under spirits (15:31–32).

Many readers meet Jubilees through the Dead Sea Scrolls, through the "Ethiopian Bible," or through popular books on angels and giants. It is none of the things popular books often make it: not a lost book of the Bible for most churches, and not a secret key. It is an ancient Jewish reading of the books of Moses, Scripture for the Ethiopian Orthodox church and a valuable witness for everyone else.

The base text. The Plain English Translation is made for this site from the Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic), the only language in which the whole book survives. The base is VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), James VanderKam's critical edition, under his verse numbers, in Ran HaCohen's transcription as published by the Open Siddur Project (CC BY-SA 4.0). It is not Dillmann's text of 1859. A copy of the same transcription on Beta maṣāḥǝft was used at first, but in about 450 verses it stops at the first full stop, so it was replaced.

Slips corrected. In six places the transcription has a slip, and the site reads the text as Dillmann's edition of 1859 has it (page images read in the Source Library): 3:20, 4:2, 4:4, 4:5, 5:27 and 34:2. These are copying faults in the digital text, not readings of VanderKam's edition, so they have no variant note.

The other witnesses. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's printed Bible is shown from its digital copy (Beta maṣāḥǝft) only where that copy is complete: it has the same fault, stopping at the first full stop in about 450 verses, and it lacks 4:3–14. It is not an independent witness after chapter 5, where it agrees with VanderKam's text word for word in almost every verse, so it is cited only where the two differ. The Latin readings (chapters 13–49 in parts; there is no Latin for chapters 1–12) and the Greek quotations of church writers and chroniclers come from R. H. Charles's edition and notes of 1902; Charles's manuscripts a, b, c and d are cited from his 1902 notes. Charles's English of 1913, which is free to use, was used only to check the sense. Charles numbers one verse fewer than VanderKam in chapters 1 and 11; the notes say where. Verses 26:32–33 are divided as Charles divides them (VanderKam's text runs them together).

Where the Plain English Translation does not follow VanderKam. Each place has a variant note naming the witness followed: 1:6 and 1:11 (the EOTC printed Bible), 12:1 (Charles's text), 13:10 (the Latin), 18:12 (one Ge'ez word left untranslated), 24:3 and 24:6 ("red" stew, Charles's correction), 29:14 (the Latin "the Salt Sea," and Akrabbim with Charles's manuscripts), 32:4 (twice) and 34:4 (the Latin), 40:4 (the Latin) and 48:17 (Dillmann's text).

Key terms are the same throughout: "the Lord" for the Ge'ez ʾƎgziʾabḥer (Ge'ez has no separate divine name, so the site's "the LORD" is kept only when Genesis or Exodus is quoted), "the angel of the presence," "the heavenly tablets," "the Watchers," "Mastema," "jubilee" for a period of 49 years and "week of years" for seven years. Places where Jubilees retells Genesis or Exodus follow the site's own wording of those books as far as the Ge'ez allows.

The book has had several names. Its opening words call it the account of the "division" of the days of the law by their weeks of years and their jubilees (1:0), and the Damascus Document refers to a book of that kind of name (CD 16:2–4). In Ge'ez it is Kufale, "Division," and the Ethiopian church's list calls it "Jublee" and "the Little Genesis." Greek writers called it Iobēlaia, "Jubilees," and much more often hē leptē Genesis, "the Little Genesis": Charles counted sixteen uses in Epiphanius, Syncellus, Cedrenus, Zonaras and Glycas. "Little" does not mean short. Jubilees is longer than Genesis; Charles explains the word as "detailed," because it gives the fine points the Bible leaves out. Jerome called it Mikrogenesis. Some Byzantine writers say it was also called the Apocalypse of Moses, and the Latin Gelasian Decree knows it as "the Book of the Daughters of Adam, that is, Leptogenesis" (Charles 1902).

sections.h: The Sinai frame and the heavenly tablets
sections.b:
The book opens on 16 of the third month of the first year after the Exodus, when God calls Moses up the mountain to receive the stone tablets (1:1, building on Exodus 24:12–18). During the forty days God shows Moses the past and the future, tells him that Israel will turn away and then return, and orders the angel of the presence to write for Moses from creation until the sanctuary is built among them forever (1:27). Then the angel takes "the tablets of the division of the years" and speaks (1:29–2:1). From there on the narrator is "we," the angels who were present at creation and at every event.

So there are two sets of tablets: the stone tablets of the law Moses brings down, and the heavenly tablets, a record in heaven of laws, dates and destinies, from which the angel reads. The heavenly tablets hold the law of birth purity (3:10), the Feast of Weeks (6:17), the 364-day year (6:29–30), the punishment of Israelites who give a daughter to a foreigner (30:9), tithes (32:15) and the friendship of Abraham with God (19:9). The idea builds on Exodus 24:12 and 31:18 and is shared with 1 Enoch's "heavenly tablets." It lets the writer say that what he teaches is not new but older than Moses.

Jubilees insists on a year of exactly 364 days, 52 weeks, divided into four quarters of thirteen weeks, with a day of remembrance at the start of each (6:23–32). Because 364 is divisible by seven, every date falls on the same day of the week every year, so each feast falls on the same weekday every year. The angel warns that people will watch the moon, which "comes ten days early, year after year," and so will confuse the feasts (6:36–38). This is a direct attack on reckoning by the moon. Grintz describes the scheme as months of thirty days, with the third, sixth, ninth and twelfth months having thirty-one, and four new years. Jubilees says Enoch was the first to write down the signs of heaven and the order of the months (4:17–18), and the Astronomical Book of 1 Enoch (72–82) has a related 364-day year.

The same 364-day calendar appears in Qumran texts, including the Temple Scroll (VanderKam 1992), which is one reason scholars link the book to the movement behind the scrolls. The rabbis, by contrast, kept a calendar tied to the moon, and Charles notes that the medieval Samaritan Chronicle argues against reckoning by the sun alone. The 364-day year does not match the real solar year of about 365¼ days, so it would drift unless corrected; Jubilees never says how.

sections.h: Jubilees, 1 Enoch and the Levi traditions
sections.b:
Jubilees knows Enoch's books. It says Enoch was the first person to learn writing, wrote down the signs of heaven, saw in a dream what was and what will be, and wrote his testimony (4:17–19), and that in Eden he still writes down the judgment of the world (4:23). VanderKam notes that 4:19 may refer to the Dream Visions of 1 Enoch (83–90). The two books share the Watchers and their giant children, but tell it differently: in 1 Enoch the Watchers come down on Mount Hermon to sin (1 Enoch 6:6), while in Jubilees they are sent down in the days of Jared "to teach humankind" and to do justice and uprightness, and only later sin (4:15; 5:1). Charles also thought the Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–104) used Jubilees; that dating of the Epistle is not the usual view today.

Jubilees also shares a body of tradition about Levi with the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs and the Aramaic Levi Document: Levi's zeal at Shechem (30), his blessing as priest (31:13–17) and his ordination at Bethel (32:1–9). Charles thought Jubilees and the Testaments both drew independently on the same sources. Scholars who reconstruct the Aramaic Levi Document (Jonas Greenfield and Michael Stone, Robert Kugler) compare one of its fragments with the law against intermarriage in 30:5–17, and Kugler used Jubilees 30:1–32:9 as a witness to the Levi traditions, as Marinus de Jonge reports. Which text borrowed from which is still argued.

sections.h: The Ethiopian Bible and Beta Israel
sections.b:
Only the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts Jubilees as Scripture today. Its published list of 81 books names "Jublee" thirteenth among the 46 books of the Old Testament, before Enoch, and explains it as "the book of Jubilee (Kufale, i.e. Division) otherwise known as the Little Genesis." VanderKam (1992) likewise says the book "enjoyed canonical status in the Abyssinian church." Like the rest of the Ethiopian Old Testament, the Ge'ez text was translated from Greek: Charles points to Greek words and Greek spellings of names left in it.

Ethiopia's Jews, the Beta Israel, also kept the Ge'ez Jubilees. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says it had "a particularly great influence" on them, and that their ritual and their calendar, especially the date of Shavuot (the Feast of Weeks), are based on it. That is a striking survival: a Jewish community whose festival dates follow, in part, a book that the rabbis set aside.

Jubilees was written in Hebrew. Hebrew fragments of it were found in at least five of the Qumran caves (1, 2, 3, 4 and 11), and the Cave 4 copies were published by James VanderKam and J. T. Milik in the Discoveries in the Judaean Desert series (volume 13, 1994). From Hebrew it was put into Greek. The Greek is lost, but many church writers and Byzantine chroniclers quoted it. From Greek it was translated into Latin and into Ge'ez. About a quarter survives in a Latin palimpsest (a reused parchment whose first writing was scraped off and written over), first published by Ceriani in 1861. Only the Ge'ez has the whole book. The canon section below gives the witnesses in more detail.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the whole book is one great jubilee
spec.body: Leviticus makes the fiftieth year the Jubilee: "Each of you will go back to his own holding" (Leviticus 25:10). Jubilees counts history from creation to the entry into Canaan as exactly fifty jubilees of 49 years, 2,450 years (Charles notes the symmetry; see 50:4). In 8:10–9:15 the land between Lebanon and Egypt falls by lot to Shem, and in 10:29–34 Canaan settles in it anyway, against his father's warning. Put together, Israel's conquest of Canaan becomes the great jubilee of world history: the land goes back to the rightful heir at the end of the fiftieth jubilee, as a field goes back to its owner in Leviticus. If this is right, the book's dates are not a timetable for its own sake but an argument that Israel's claim to the land is a release, not a theft. The symmetry is Charles's observation; the link with the Canaan story and Leviticus 25 is my framing.

spec.title: Claude's theory: angels as writers explain a New Testament commonplace
spec.body: Stephen, Paul and Hebrews all take it for granted that the law came through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2), though Exodus says God spoke the Ten Commandments himself. Charles called Jubilees "the earliest authority" for the idea. My suggestion is narrower: Jubilees may show why the idea felt natural. In it an angel does not just carry the law; he reads it to Moses from a written record in heaven (1:27–2:1). A reader who knew that picture could speak of the law as "arranged through angels" without thinking it lowered the law, and Paul, who does use the angels to set the law below the promise (Galatians 3:17–19), would be pressing a picture his hearers already knew. The textual links are Charles's; the reading of how the picture worked is mine.

prompts: The angel dictates to Moses on Sinai (1:27–2:1)

A mountain summit wrapped in cloud and fire; Moses, an old man with a long beard, sits on a rock writing on a long scroll across his knees; beside him a tall winged figure of light holds open a pair of great glowing tablets covered with rows of small marks and reads from them; below, far down the slope, the tents of Israel's camp in a desert valley at dawn.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. reading: R. H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees, or the Little Genesis (1902)
The classic translation and commentary, now in the public domain. Its dating has been revised, but its notes on the Latin, the Greek quotations and Jewish parallels are still the place to start.
R. H. Charles, The Ethiopic Version of the Hebrew Book of Jubilees (1895)
Charles's Ge'ez text from four manuscripts, with every Hebrew, Syriac, Greek and Latin fragment then known printed in full.
James C. VanderKam, The Book of Jubilees: A Critical Text (1989)
The modern critical edition of the Ge'ez, with a translation volume.
James C. VanderKam and J. T. Milik, the Jubilees fragments in Qumran Cave 4.VIII: Parabiblical Texts, Part 1 (DJD 13, 1994)
The official edition of the Hebrew copies from Cave 4.

views: Yes. The church's own list of its 81 canonical books names "Jublee" among the 46 books of the Old Testament, and explains it as "the book of Jubilee (Kufale, i.e. Division) otherwise known as the Little Genesis." VanderKam (1992) likewise speaks of its "canonical status in the Abyssinian church."

No, for the Coptic Orthodox Church. The Coptic Orthodox Diocese of Los Angeles lists the deuterocanonical books as Tobit, Judith, the additions to Esther, the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, the additions to Daniel, 1 and 2 Maccabees and Psalm 151. Jubilees is not among them.

No. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named the books outside the Hebrew canon that it counted "genuine parts of Scripture": Wisdom of Solomon, Judith, Tobit, the stories of the Dragon and of Susanna, the Maccabees and Sirach. Jubilees is not among them. Byzantine chroniclers such as George Syncellus and George Cedrenus quoted "the Little Genesis" as a source for early history, not as Scripture (Charles 1902).

No. The Council of Trent (1546) listed the books of the Old Testament, and Jubilees is not among them. Earlier, the Gelasian Decree, a Latin list credited to Pope Gelasius and probably compiled in the 500s, listed "the Book of the Daughters of Adam, that is, Leptogenesis" among the books not to be received, calling it apocryphal; Charles identifies this with Jubilees.

No. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists the canonical books and also the other books that the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not use "to establish any doctrine." Jubilees is in neither list.

No. The Westminster Confession (1.2–3) lists the books of the Old Testament from Genesis to Malachi as "given by inspiration of God," and says that the books commonly called Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of Scripture." Jubilees is not even among those Apocrypha.

canon.summary: Jubilees is Scripture for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which keeps it in its Old Testament as Kufale, and it shaped the calendar of the Beta Israel, Ethiopia's Jews. Jews, Catholics, the Eastern Orthodox and Protestants do not count it as Scripture, though it was copied among the Dead Sea Scrolls and many early church writers knew it as "the Little Genesis."
accepted_by: Scripture. Hebrew fragments were found in at least five of the caves, Caves 1, 2, 3, 4 and 11 (the Israel Antiquities Authority's Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library, whose Discovery Sites page names Jubilees for Caves 2 and 3 and whose manuscript pages include "1Q Jubilees," "4Q Jubilees" and "11Q Jubilees"), and the Damascus Document, a rule book of the same movement, sends its readers to "the Book of Time Divisions by Jubilees and Weeks" (CD 16:2–4, Cook's translation). VanderKam (1992) counted fragments of twelve manuscripts; Matthew Monger (2014) argues that "there were likely not 14 complete manuscripts of Jubilees at Qumran," and Devorah Dimant has questioned whether the Damascus Document's words are a quotation of Jubilees. Whether they counted it as Scripture in the later sense cannot be settled, since there was no closed list yet.

Not Scripture. It is not in the Hebrew Bible, and its calendar and laws differ from the rabbis': Charles shows that its strict Sabbath laws (no marital relations, no war, 50:8–12) and its rule on circumcision exactly on the eighth day were later eased in the Mishnah, and its 364-day year opposes reckoning by the moon. Parts of its stories still reached medieval Hebrew works such as Midrash Tadshe and the Book of Jashar.
The early church and the Byzantine writers

Known and used, but not as Scripture. Didymus of Alexandria and Epiphanius cite it by name as the Little Genesis, Jerome knew it, and Byzantine chroniclers from George Syncellus to Michael Glycas drew on it for the early history of the world. The Gelasian Decree, a Latin list credited to Pope Gelasius and probably compiled in the 500s, lists "the Book of the Daughters of Adam, that is, Leptogenesis" as apocryphal (all as Charles 1902 collects them).
Not Scripture. It is not among the books the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named as "genuine parts of Scripture" beyond the Hebrew canon, and no Greek manuscript of it survives, only quotations.
Coptic, Syriac and Armenian Orthodox churches

Not Scripture for the Coptic Orthodox Church: the Coptic Orthodox Diocese of Los Angeles lists ten deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, the additions to Esther, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the additions to Daniel, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Psalm 151), and Jubilees is not one of them. For the Syriac and Armenian churches, the evidence here is Charles's on the versions: he (1902) knew of no Coptic or Armenian version, and for Syriac only a short list, "Names of the Wives of the Patriarchs according to the Hebrew Book called Jubilees," in a British Museum manuscript; he judged the evidence for a Syriac version "not conclusive."
Not Scripture. Not in the canon defined at Trent (1546), and the Gelasian Decree calls it apocryphal. Catholic scholars study it as background.
Not Scripture, and not among the Apocrypha that some Protestants read for instruction: neither Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles nor the Westminster Confession names it.

provenance.b:
Jubilees is the work of one Jewish author who wrote in Hebrew in the 100s BC, drawing on older books and traditions (Charles 1902, §13). The usual dates today come from three kinds of evidence. The Qumran copies: the oldest then published were dated by their handwriting to about 100 BC, so the book is older than that (VanderKam 1992). Its sources: it uses Genesis and Exodus throughout and seems to know 1 Enoch, perhaps the Dream Visions of about 164 BC (4:19). Possible allusions: some see the Maccabean wars in the battles against the Amorites and Edom (34:1–9; 37–38) and the persecution of Antiochus in the vision of chapter 23; others think these can be read otherwise.

  • About 170–140 BC: VanderKam (1992), now the most common view.
  • Before 167 BC: Nickelsburg and Goldstein (as VanderKam reports them).
  • About 150 BC: Bohn (1900), as Charles reports him.
  • 135 to about 105 BC: Charles (1902), under John Hyrcanus; Grintz (Encyclopaedia Judaica) at the end of Hyrcanus's reign.
  • First century AD: Dillmann, Rönsch, Singer and Schürer, before the Dead Sea Scrolls; now given up.

Hebrew. Charles argued for it before the scrolls were found: a book claiming to come from Moses would be written in Hebrew, which the book itself calls the language of creation (12:25–26); its puzzling phrases make sense when put back into Hebrew; it keeps Hebrew turns of speech and word plays on names; and medieval Hebrew works preserve passages of it. The Qumran fragments, which are in Hebrew, confirmed this (Grintz). Charles also explained the Aramaic-looking name forms in the Latin as the translator's habit.

Fragments of Jubilees were found in at least five Qumran caves. The Israel Antiquities Authority's Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library names Jubilees among the finds of Cave 2 and a copy in Cave 3, and has manuscript pages titled "1Q Jubilees" (1Q17), "4Q Jubilees" (4Q216) and "11Q Jubilees" (11Q12), so copies come from Caves 1, 2, 3, 4 and 11. VanderKam and J. T. Milik published the Cave 4 copies in Qumran Cave 4.VIII (DJD 13, 1994), for example 4QJubilees c (4Q218). In 1992 VanderKam counted fragments of twelve manuscripts and dated the two oldest then published, 4Q216 and 4Q217, to about 100 BC; a fragment once reported from Masada turned out not to be Jubilees. How many separate copies there really were is debated: Matthew Monger (2014), studying 4Q216 as a physical object, argues that "there were likely not 14 complete manuscripts of Jubilees at Qumran," and questions the common view that the Qumran Hebrew and the much later Ge'ez agree closely.

No Greek manuscript survives, but the Greek was widely read. Charles lists quotations or uses in Origen, Diodorus of Antioch, Isidore of Pelusium, Epiphanius, John Malala, Anastasius of Sinai (in Latin), George Syncellus, George Cedrenus, the Suda, Zonaras, Michael Glycas and Joel, and scholia in a Greek manuscript of Genesis. Syncellus, for example, says that "the Little Genesis" tells how Mastema, the ruler of the demons, proposed Abraham's test (17:16). The Greek forms of Mastema's name are Μαστιφάμ (Syncellus) and Μαστιφάτ (Cedrenus). Both the Latin and the Ge'ez were translated from this Greek (Charles 1902, §§7–8).

About a quarter of the book survives in Latin, in a single palimpsest manuscript, first published by Ceriani in 1861, then by Hermann Rönsch (1874) and by Charles (1895). It covers parts of chapters 13 to 49 and none of chapters 1 to 12. Rönsch thought it was made in or near Egypt by a Palestinian Jew in the 400s. Charles judged it "almost of equal value with the Ethiopic" where it survives, though more corrected by later scribes toward the Greek and Latin Bibles; in many places it keeps the true text where the Ge'ez has lost it.

Only Ge'ez has the whole book. Charles called this version "most accurate and trustworthy and indeed as a rule servilely literal," with the usual copying slips (repeated words, small gaps) and a few places brought into line with the Ge'ez Genesis. He knew four manuscripts in Europe: a (Paris) and b (British Museum), of the 1400s and 1500s, and c (Tübingen) and d (d'Abbadie collection), both recent; he thought b the most trustworthy. August Dillmann published the first Ge'ez edition in 1859 from c and d; Charles's edition of 1895 used all four. By 1992 VanderKam could count 27 copies, and his critical text of 1989 is the modern standard edition.

For Syriac there is only a list, "Names of the Wives of the Patriarchs according to the Hebrew Book called Jubilees" (British Museum Add. 12,154), first published by Ceriani in 1861; Charles thought the evidence for a full Syriac version "not conclusive." VanderKam (1992) adds that an anonymous Syriac chronicle reproduces about 137 verses in 29 citations, "if there ever was" a Syriac version. Medieval Hebrew works such as Midrash Tadshe, the Book of Jashar and the Chronicles of Jerahmeel preserve stories from Jubilees (Charles 1902, §§9 and 22).

rejected_why.b: Jubilees never entered the Hebrew Bible, and its teaching ran against the way the rabbis came to keep the law. Its year of 364 days by the sun conflicts with a calendar kept by the moon, and the book calls watching the moon a path to error (6:36–38). Its laws are stricter than the Mishnah's: it forbids marital relations and war on the Sabbath and makes death the penalty for both (50:8–13), and Charles shows that the Mishnah and later teachers eased such rules. It sets the start of the law in heaven and in the patriarchs, and gives an angel the role of revealing it (1:27).

Christian writers quoted it and drew on it for early history, as a source rather than as Scripture (Charles 1902). It was not part of the Greek Old Testament that the church received from the Jews, so its claim to come from Sinai stood without support from Israel's Scripture or from any Jewish community that read it publicly. The Gelasian Decree, a Latin list credited to Pope Gelasius and probably compiled in the 500s, listed "the Book of the Daughters of Adam, that is, Leptogenesis" among the apocrypha. Later lists of the Old Testament, whether Catholic (Trent, 1546), Orthodox (Jerusalem, 1672) or Protestant (the Thirty-Nine Articles; Westminster), do not include it at all.

Readers who set it aside, then and now, point to several things. (1) It adds to Moses. It claims that Moses wrote a second, fuller account on Sinai, which Exodus never mentions. (2) Its law binds the patriarchs. It makes Noah, Abraham and Jacob keep feasts and rules that the Torah first gives at Sinai, and it says nations other than Israel were never meant to keep the Sabbath (2:31). Paul reads the order the other way, with the promise to Abraham long before the law (Galatians 3:17). (3) Its calendar. It makes a 364-day year a command of heaven, though no such year matches the sky, and the Bible's feasts are tied to new moons. (4) Its sharp line against the nations. It orders death for the Israelite man who gives his daughter or sister to a foreigner, and for the woman (30:7–10), and forbids taking foreign wives (30:11). The 66 books also tell of Ruth, Rahab and the foreign wives of Joseph and Moses. The tension is inside Jubilees too: it keeps Joseph's marriage to Asenath, the daughter of Potiphar, priest of Heliopolis (44:24), and names Canaanite wives for Simeon and Judah (34:20).

Modern scholars of every church, and of none, give historical reasons. Pseudonymity: the book speaks in the name of Moses and an angel, as other Jewish writings of the period spoke in the names of ancient heroes. Date: its laws and its concerns (the Greek games, circumcision, the calendar, wars with Edom) belong to the 100s BC. Dependence: it is built on the finished books of Genesis and Exodus, often quoting them word for word, and on 1 Enoch. These are reasons it is not by Moses, not reasons it is worthless.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts it among the 46 books of its Old Testament. No other church's list opened here names it (Trent, Jerusalem 1672, the Thirty-Nine Articles, Westminster, and the Coptic list). For a church that reads its Old Testament with the Orit, the books of Moses, Jubilees fills in what Moses was shown on the mountain. At Qumran, the copies and the Damascus Document's reference show that a Jewish movement before Christ held it in high regard, and the Beta Israel kept it into modern times.

cited_in.b: Genesis is the source here: Jubilees retells Genesis 1 to Exodus 24 and depends on those books, not they on it. Certain. It follows Genesis closely, often word for word, and Charles shows that its Hebrew text of Genesis in a number of places agrees with the Septuagint or the Samaritan Pentateuch against the Masoretic Text. Ethiopian Orthodox readers see the relation as two accounts of the same revelation to Moses.

Exodus is the source: it gives the frame of the whole book. Exodus tells of Moses called up the mountain to receive the stone tablets and staying forty days and forty nights; Jubilees sets itself in those forty days (1:1–4) and claims to be what was revealed there. Certain.

"You were given the law by the orders of angels" (Acts 7:53), with Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2. Exodus does not say this. Charles called Jubilees "the earliest authority" for the idea, since in it the angel of the presence writes and recites the law to Moses (1:27; 2:1). The New Testament writers need not have read Jubilees: the idea could have been shared in the Judaism of their day. A real background, not a citation. Moderate.

See the entry on Acts 7:53: the law "arranged through angels." Paul uses the idea to rank the law below the promise, the opposite of Jubilees, where the law is eternal and the angels keep it in heaven. Moderate, as for Acts 7:53.
"The word spoken through angels" (Hebrews 2:2). The same shared tradition as Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19. Moderate.

Stephen says Jacob and the fathers were moved to Shechem and buried in the tomb Abraham bought. Genesis says only that Joseph's bones were brought up (Genesis 50:25; Joshua 24:32). Jubilees 46:9 says the Israelites took up the bones of all of Jacob's sons except Joseph and buried them in the double cave, and Charles called this "the oldest source of the tradition in Acts." But Jubilees buries them at Machpelah, not Shechem, so the link is a shared idea about the other sons' bones, not the same tradition. Charles proposed the link; the different burial place counts against it. Weak to moderate.

Stephen says Moses was about forty when he went to see his people, and spent forty years in Midian (Acts 7:23, 30). Exodus gives no age. Jubilees dates both events (47:10–12; 48:1) with different numbers, which Charles calls the oldest dates on the subject. Charles proposed the link; the numbers differ, which counts against it. A sign that Jews were already filling in Moses' life with dates, not a source of Stephen's numbers. Weak.

"He was called the friend of God" (James 2:23). Jubilees says Abraham "was found faithful" and was written on the heavenly tablets as the friend of the Lord (19:9), and also cites Genesis 15:6 (14:6). Both rest on Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7, which call Abraham God's friend. Charles lists it as a parallel; James quotes Genesis, not Jubilees. Weak as a link to Jubilees.

James says God "tempts no one himself" (James 1:13), yet in Genesis 22:1, God tests Abraham. Jubilees deals with the same problem by having Prince Mastema propose the test (17:16), as Satan does in Job 1–2. Charles saw the same concern in both. A shared question, not a borrowing. Weak as a link.

"In the Lord's sight one day is like a thousand years" (2 Peter 3:8). Jubilees uses the same idea to explain why Adam died on the day he ate the fruit: he lived 930 years, short of a thousand, and "a thousand years are one day in the testimony of the heavens" (4:30). Both build on Psalm 90:4. Charles called Jubilees the oldest such statement; 2 Peter applies it to the delay of the Lord's coming instead. Moderate as a shared idea; no sign of direct use.

Angels who did not keep their position, kept in chains for judgment (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4). Jubilees has the angels who sinned bound in the depths of the earth until the great judgment (5:6, 10), in a story it shares with 1 Enoch 6–16, which Jude quotes. The link runs mainly through 1 Enoch; Jubilees is a second witness to the same tradition. Moderate, through 1 Enoch.

The scribes say Jesus throws out demons "with the help of the ruler of the demons" (Mark 3:22; compare Matthew 12:24). Jubilees knows an organized realm of evil spirits under a single chief, Mastema, who keeps a tenth of them to lead people astray (10:8–9). Charles lists the parallel. It shows the belief was old by Jesus' day; it does not show the Gospels used Jubilees. Moderate as background.

Jesus speaks of the little ones' angels in heaven (Matthew 18:10; compare Acts 12:15). Charles says Jubilees is the first book to mention a guardian angel of an individual: Rebekah is told that Jacob's guardian is greater than Esau's (35:17). Background only; weak as a link.

Revelation calls believers "a kingdom, priests" (Revelation 1:6; Revelation 5:10), where Exodus 19:6 has "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation." Jubilees 16:18 also makes two nouns of it: the Ge'ez has mängəśtä wäkhənätä, "a kingdom and a priesthood," which the Plain English Translation gives as "a kingdom, a priesthood and a holy people" (Charles's English of 1913 has "a kingdom and priests and a holy nation"). Charles lists the parallel. Both could come straight from the Hebrew of Exodus, so the link is weak.

Revelation's angels who hold back the winds, the angel over fire and the angel of the waters (Revelation 7:1; Revelation 14:18; Revelation 16:5) match the classes of angels Jubilees says God made on the first day, over winds, fire, clouds and seasons (2:2). Charles lists it; a shared Jewish picture of angels over nature. Moderate as background.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how Jews read Genesis and Exodus in the 100s BC, Jubilees is among the most valuable books we have: it was copied at Qumran, named by the Damascus Document, and shows ideas the New Testament takes for granted, such as the law given through angels and an organized realm of demons. As a text, it survives complete only in a Ge'ez translation of a Greek translation of a Hebrew original, but the Latin, the Greek quotations and the Hebrew fragments let scholars check parts of it. As history, its claim to be what an angel dictated to Moses on Sinai is not supported by the evidence, which points to a Jewish priestly writer of the 100s BC; the Ethiopian Orthodox church receives it as part of its Old Testament nonetheless. Measured against the 66 books, it follows Genesis and Exodus closely in its stories, goes well beyond them in dates, laws and angels, and in a few places conflicts with them.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish belief before Jesus: very high
sections.b: Here no one doubts its value. Qumran copies prove it was being copied by about 100 BC, and the Damascus Document refers to it. It is, in Charles's words, the oldest commentary on Genesis we have. It shows how a learned, priestly circle in Judea thought about the law, the calendar, angels and demons, the nations, and the last days, two centuries before the New Testament. Ideas the New Testament mentions without explaining, such as the law "arranged through angels" (Galatians 3:19), a ruler of the demons (Mark 3:22), guardian angels (Matthew 18:10) and a day of the Lord as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8), already appear in it. For the world of Jesus and Paul, and for the Dead Sea Scrolls, it is essential reading.

Mixed, but better than it first looks. The whole book exists only in Ge'ez, made from a lost Greek translation, and the oldest Ge'ez manuscripts known to Charles were of the 1400s and 1500s, more than fifteen centuries after the book was written. Against that, there are checks: the Latin covers about a quarter of the book (chapters 13–49 in parts), the Greek quotations cover scattered verses, and the Hebrew fragments from Qumran cover others. Charles judged the Ge'ez version very literal and careful. The common view is that the Qumran Hebrew and the Ge'ez agree closely where they overlap; Monger questions how close. In practice, the sense of most verses is secure, while exact wording and the many numbers (dates, ages, years) are less so, and the variant notes say where the witnesses differ.

sections.h: 3. The claim to come from Sinai
sections.b: The book says an angel dictated it to Moses on the mountain from the heavenly tablets. The historical evidence points the other way. It argues about questions of the 100s BC (the Greek games, circumcision, the calendar, marriage to Gentiles, the Edomites), it builds on the finished books of Genesis and Exodus and on 1 Enoch, and it first appears in Hebrew copies of about 100 BC. Most scholars see a learned priest who put his teaching in Moses' mouth, a common practice of the time, and not necessarily a deception: he was claiming that his teaching was what the Torah truly meant. The Ethiopian Orthodox reading, in its strongest form: the church has received the book in its Old Testament, and what was shown to Moses on the mountain during forty days need not be limited to the chapters of Exodus; a late copy does not prove a late origin. A fair summary: the evidence of content, sources and copies strongly favors a writer of the 100s BC, and the traditional view rests on the church's reception of the book rather than on historical evidence.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: one God who created all things in six days and rested on the seventh (2; Genesis 1–2); the stories of the patriarchs and the Exodus, which it mostly retells faithfully; God's covenant with Abraham and his choice of Israel (15; Genesis 17); the Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel (2:17–33; Exodus 31:13–17); the hope that God will give his people a new heart and that they will be his children (1:23–25; Deuteronomy 30:6; Ezekiel 36:26).
  • Goes beyond: exact dates for every event in jubilees; the heavenly tablets as a written law older than Sinai; angels created on the first day, and the angels of the presence as the narrators; Mastema and his tenth of the spirits; Enoch as the first writer; the patriarchs keeping the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Booths; the Day of Atonement explained by Joseph's brothers' grief (34:18–19); many names of wives and places not in Genesis.
  • Changes: it smooths out what readers found troubling, for example making Mastema, not God, propose Abraham's test (17:16; compare Genesis 22:1), giving Levi the first blessing and Judah the second (31:13–20), where Genesis 49:5–7 curses Levi's anger (Charles saw Levi set over Judah here), and turning Levi and Simeon's attack on Shechem, which Jacob condemns (Genesis 34:30; Genesis 49:5–7), into righteous zeal (30).
  • Conflicts: its 364-day year as heaven's law, against a biblical calendar of new moons (Numbers 28:11–14); its claim that the Sabbath and the law were binding on the patriarchs, which sits uneasily with Paul's argument that the law came 430 years after the promise (Galatians 3:17); and its death penalty for the man who gives his daughter or sister to a Gentile (30:7), though Jubilees itself keeps Joseph's Egyptian wife (44:24). Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read such places within the church's tradition; other churches see them as the marks of a human book.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you belong to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, it is part of your Old Testament, and your church's teachers are your guide. If you belong to another church, it is not Scripture for you, but it is an ancient and serious Jewish reading of the books of Moses, older than the New Testament. Either way, read it with respect, and do not treat it as a secret key to the Bible.

how_to_read.h: Read it beside Genesis and Exodus
how_to_read.b: Jubilees makes sense only next to the books it retells. Read a chapter of Genesis, then the matching chapter of Jubilees, and ask what it added, left out or changed, and why. The "echo" and "Compared with the Bible" notes do this verse by verse.

how_to_read.h: Read it in its own time
how_to_read.b: Its strong laws about the Sabbath, circumcision, nakedness, the calendar and marriage were written for Jews who felt their way of life threatened by Greek culture in the 100s BC. Knowing that helps you hear its urgency without making its rules your own.

how_to_read.h: Use it for the New Testament world
how_to_read.b: Many things the New Testament mentions in passing (the law given through angels, the ruler of the demons, guardian angels, the thousand-year day, debates over days and seasons) were already part of Jewish thought, and Jubilees is one of the oldest places to see them. Use it as background, the way you would use the Dead Sea Scrolls or Josephus.

Popular books and videos sometimes present Jubilees as a "lost book" removed from the Bible, or use its 364-day calendar to set dates for feasts today. Of the church lists opened for these pages, only the Ethiopian Orthodox list names it, and its calendar does not match the sun or the moon. Weigh such claims against the evidence on these pages.
